text: Two interns and a nurse sit in front of American military police, answering for something done inside a hospital while the war was still on. The word for it is vivisection; the patients were a downed American air crew. Kei Kumai's subject is not the act but the arithmetic that precedes it — the deference a hospital runs on, orders arriving from somewhere above, a career worth keeping, and the moment a young doctor stops finding a reason to say no. It is a war film with no battlefield anywhere in it, and 123 minutes is long enough to make the ward feel like a front. The Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize went to it; at home, Kinema Junpo named it the film of the year. One jury abroad and one in Japan, agreeing about a picture that offers its own country no exit.

Casanova at one end, Dracula at the other, and 148 minutes of Catalan between them. The first stretch is candlelight and appetite: a castle, a servant newly hired, the eighteenth century still confident that it will last. Then the ground turns north, poor and dark. Albert Serra lets the runtime carry the argument — time enough for one century's idea of pleasure, talkative and rational and pleased with itself, to be worn down by an older hunger that never explains itself. Nothing is announced; the weather simply changes. It took the Golden Leopard, and Caimán's poll of the hundred best Spanish films made room for it, a Spanish canon entry spoken in Catalan. The film assumes a viewer willing to stay with a scene after its information has been delivered.

A boy is trusted with letters because nobody thinks of a boy as a witness. Leo Colston is spending the summer in the countryside, a schoolboy among people with land, and he is half in love with Marian, who is an aristocrat, which is precisely what makes him useful to her: he can cross a field to Ted Burgess's farm and back and attract no comment. Joseph Losey lets the English landscape do the class work, since in that country the question of who may walk where is never only about walking. The screenplay took a BAFTA, one performance took an Academy Award, and the BFI later placed the film among the hundred best British pictures. What the citations leave out is the cruelty of the arrangement: the errand is the part of an adult affair handed to whoever is small enough to be trusted with it, and small enough not to count.

The film runs 111 minutes and so, more or less, does the morning it depicts. Real time is not a style here but the whole method, and it forbids nearly everything a drama normally does: the introductions that tell an audience whom to care about, the pause for context, the retrospective line explaining what this will come to mean. Paul Greengrass made it five years after the day itself, and the discipline of the form is his answer to the obvious objection — nobody in the picture is allowed to know more than the people did. What the passengers on United 93 learn, the audience learns at the same minute. It is filed as a thriller and is quietly hostile to the label; suspense wants outcomes in doubt, and this one had been settled long before the first ticket was sold.

A husband decides his wife's unhappiness is an engineering problem, and his solution is to find her a lover. Raoul means it kindly, which is the joke and also the trouble: his generosity is total, unembarrassed and conducted entirely between men. He recruits Stéphane, who proves equally certain that Solange is a puzzle with a male answer, and the two settle into a long, courteous, wholly serious negotiation about what would make a woman feel better, while she declines to improve. Bertrand Blier plays it straight for as long as he can. The Academy's international-feature award went to it and the National Society of Film Critics called it the best picture of 1978 — prizes that now double as a record of what a comedy was once permitted to find funny.

The murders happened; the men sent to solve them are the film's heroes; everything else follows from that arrangement. Alan Parker takes the killing of civil rights workers in the 1960s South and hands it to two FBI agents — one schooled in Bureau procedure, one a former small-town sheriff who knows what a county will and will not say aloud — so that the central conflict of a film about segregation is a disagreement between two federal outsiders about method. It works. Parker directs it as a thriller and it functions as one, the town closing ranks, the silence thickening, while the Black residents whose danger set all of it in motion stand mostly as the ground the argument is conducted on. The National Board of Review named it the best film of 1988 and a Silver Bear went to one of its leads. The unease that comes with it is not a failure of the craft; it is the craft.

Ninety-two minutes is a short film about a long fear, and the fear is the ambient kind that makes institutions careful. By the early 1950s Senator Joseph McCarthy's hunt for communists ran on the premise that anyone might be asked to prove they were not one, and Edward R. Murrow's position was that a broadcaster's caution is itself an editorial act. George Clooney directs the story as procedure: what can be said, what can be sourced, who will stand behind it when the complaints arrive, how many words a man is willing to cut. There is very little action in it and a great deal of drafting. A Volpi Cup went to its lead and the National Board of Review called it the year's best film, though the particular pleasure of the thing is narrower than either citation implies, and it lives in the sound of a sentence being weighed before anyone reads it aloud.

By 2004 the Western was a form a director needed a reason to pick up. Ron Howard's reason is Maggie Gilkeson: a rancher raising two daughters alone, competent at nearly everything her life demands and wholly unequipped for what happens next, which is that the older girl is taken. The tracker she needs is the father she has not forgiven. The border is close, and what waits across it for a stolen teenage girl is a market. So the chase runs on two clocks — the distance to the line, and the time it takes two people to work together while refusing to reconcile — and Howard shoots the hard country straight while letting the family argument carry the weight. It is an odd balance to hold for 135 minutes, and the film is more interesting for trying.

A man arrives in a small town to supervise a building that does not exist yet. Na runs the hotel he checks into; Ta is the architect, sent down from the city, and for long stretches the whole event of the film is that two people are in the same quiet place at the same hours. Aditya Assarat gives that 92 minutes and very little incident. What accumulates instead is proximity, and the particular awkwardness of a town where being seen with someone is itself information that travels. He is patient with rooms: what people do while nothing is being decided, the hours a hotel has to fill. The slowness is not a mood, it is a measurement of how long two careful people take to admit anything. Meanwhile the development Ta came to build will change the place, and everyone knows it, which puts a clock on a story that appears to have none.

The literary magazine is hiring, and the applicant's real qualification is something he knows about the editor that the editor does not know about him. Lee Weon-san is a graduate student, quiet and careful and recently left by his girlfriend; the man who runs the magazine is the reason she left. The job is a way to stand next to him. What follows across 124 minutes is a very particular humiliation, and the person suffering it arranged it: proximity chosen on purpose, resentment with nowhere to put itself, an apprenticeship under a man he would like to become and would also like to ruin. Park Chan-ok keeps it all at office scale — errands, small rooms, a favour asked and granted — so that jealousy reads as a daily practice rather than an outburst. Nothing in it announces itself as a crisis, which is why it accumulates.

Crossing the border turned out to be the achievable part; everything after it is rent, work, and being from somewhere the city has opinions about. Seung-chul lives at the edges of Seoul, where the work is casual and employers can calculate exactly how little leverage a defector has. Park Jung-bum's first feature spends 127 minutes on the transactions most films skip: a wage argued down, a room found, an introduction that goes nowhere, the small daily audit of whether a man can be trusted with anything at all. The realism is not decoration; it is the argument. He has reached the country that was supposed to be the destination, and the film's patience goes to how little that settles — a life is not granted on arrival, it is assembled out of the jobs nobody else wants.

A man who spends his days repairing mannequins has two sons at home he barely speaks to. Li Ahh and Li Ohm are more or less raising themselves, and their father, Sui, is present as a fact and absent as a person. Liew Seng Tat handles this as comedy, which is the harder choice and the more accurate one: boys left alone are not sorrowful all day, they are bored, inventive, occasionally cruel, hungry at predictable times. The comedy is a matter of scale — what looks like neglect from outside is, at a child's height, simply the shape of a day. Ninety-seven minutes is enough to establish a routine and then let small things disturb it. Underneath sits the father's trade, never underlined: broken figures returned to presentable shape by a man who cannot manage the same for his household.

Penang to Kuala Lumpur is not a long journey, and it is long enough. Ping makes it in order to work for her aunt, so the city arrives as a job, a room and a set of hours rather than as freedom. John arrives as persistence: he approaches, is not encouraged, approaches again. Tan Chui Mui is exact about the distance between being pursued and being chosen, and about concessions made one at a time, each small enough to be defensible on its own. There is a boyfriend still up north, kept in view less as a rival than as a measure of how far she has travelled from herself. Ninety minutes, in Chinese, with almost nothing raised above speaking volume. What stands to be lost is not a relationship but a young woman's private estimate of what she is worth to somebody.

A woman sleeps through the fall of the Berlin Wall, and her son decides she will go on sleeping through it. Her heart will not take a shock, and she believed, sincerely and in public, in the state that has just stopped existing, so Alex reassembles it for her inside one apartment: the correct groceries, the correct news, a country shrunk to the size of a bedroom and kept running by one exhausted young man on a budget. Wolfgang Becker plays the deception for comedy and lets the cost gather at the edges, because every prop Alex has to find is a small piece of research into what his mother's life was actually made of. The European Film Awards named it the year's best film; the German Film Award did the same at home. A comedy of set dressing, in which the set is a country.
